async-io.summary: Event-driven servers multiplex many connections onto few threads by waiting for readiness (epoll, kqueue) or completion (IOCP, io_uring) and running short, non-blocking handlers. They only scale if nothing blocks the loop, buffers are bounded, and cancellation and timeouts flow through the whole call tree.
points: Thread-per-connection pays stack memory and context switches for every idle connection; event loops spend work only on ready sockets (the C10K problem).
Readiness APIs (select, poll, epoll, kqueue) say an operation can start; completion APIs (IOCP, io_uring) perform it and report the result. Reactor vs proactor.
Edge-triggered epoll needs non-blocking descriptors and draining until EAGAIN; level-triggered EPOLLOUT must be enabled only while output is queued.
A loop runs one callback at a time: CPU work, synchronous DNS or file I/O inside a handler stalls every client. Offload it to a bounded worker pool.
async/await compiles to resumable state machines; it gives concurrency at await points, not parallelism, and async-ness spreads to callers (coloured functions).
Backpressure keeps memory bounded: bounded queues, pausing reads, TCP flow control, and pull-based request(n) protocols make the slowest stage set the pace.
Structured concurrency and deadline propagation make task lifetimes, errors and cancellation explicit, so shutdown can drain work and failures are never lost.
traps: Marking CPU-bound code async does not make it run in parallel; it still blocks the loop until it awaits.
Cancelling an await on a thread-pool call does not stop the thread; the blocking work keeps running and keeps its side effects.
A non-blocking send() can accept only part of the data; unsent bytes must be buffered and retried when the socket becomes writable.
